passage:
Pema, you're the friend I dropped, so you deserve to hear this from me.
The year I turned twenty, I got robbed near the station, and something in me went hard. I found a channel that explained everything. At first they said "those people". Within months it was "animals", "an infestation". I watched it every night, nothing else. When you said, "They're not all the same, Tanuja," I muted you. Then I muted everyone who said anything like that.
The moment it cracked was small. A delivery man mixed up our flat number, and I heard myself say to my flatmate, "One of those things again."
Things. I'd called a person a thing, and it hadn't even felt strange.
I sat on the stairs a long time after that. I unfollowed the channel that night. I'm still angry about being robbed. I'm just not willing to stop seeing people.
So, sorry. Can we get chai?

qa.q: What did Tanuja call the delivery man?
qa.a: Tanuja said, "One of those things again."

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel on the stairs after hearing those words?
qa.a: Tanuja felt shaken and ashamed, realising that calling a person a thing had not even felt strange.

qa.q: What turning point shows the value of noticing dehumanising language?
qa.a: Hearing the word "things" about a real person showed Tanuja how far the channel had pulled, and Tanuja unfollowed it that night.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Pema to be muted?
qa.a: Pema lost a friend simply for saying people are not all the same, which likely hurt, and now has to decide whether to accept Tanuja's apology.

grounding: Tanuja drifts into one-channel content that turns a group into animals and drops Pema for disagreeing, until Tanuja notices having called a person a thing.

passage:
I've known Kavitha since the first week of college. This is what I saw over the last year, from the outside.
In autumn, after her family's shop was vandalised, she started sending me videos from one channel. Loud host, red captions. I didn't think much of it.
By winter she'd stopped watching anything else. She left our film club group. She unfollowed people who argued with her, including me for a while.
The words changed too, slowly. First, "they're wrong". Then, "they're all the same". Then one day in the canteen: "They're not even human, Ira."
I didn't shout. I said, "You used to say nobody is just one thing." She went quiet and stirred her tea for a long time.
I honestly don't know what she was thinking. But the next week she came back to film club, and sat next to me.

qa.q: What did Kavitha say in the canteen?
qa.a: Kavitha said, "They're not even human, Ira."

qa.q: What might Kavitha have been feeling after Ira's reply?
qa.a: Kavitha may have felt caught between hurt and doubt, stirring her tea in silence, though Ira admits not knowing what she was thinking.

qa.q: What made Ira's reply in the canteen a wise one?
qa.a: Ira did not shout or argue; reminding Kavitha of her own old belief invited her to notice the dehumanising words herself.

qa.q: How has the change affected Ira?
qa.a: Ira was unfollowed for a while and watched someone known since the first week of college slip away, but Ira stayed calm and available, which left a way back.

grounding: Ira watches Kavitha, hurt after her family's shop was vandalised, consume one channel, drop people who disagree and begin to call a group less than human.

passage:
Mentor's note, second-year engineering, 12 February
Uma has been in my mentoring group since first year. This term she has changed. She used to debate happily with everyone. Last week, when Farhan disagreed with her about a news story, she said, "People like him defend those parasites," and moved to another table. She now calls a whole community "rats" and "a disease" as if describing the weather. Her laptop is always playing the same channel's videos, one after another.
Farhan told me she has unfollowed him and two other friends.
I noticed something else. When I asked about her grades, which have fallen, her eyes filled up.
What I did next: I didn't argue about the videos. I told her that calling people rats is the kind of language that comes before cruelty, and that I was worried about her. I asked her to meet the college counsellor with me on Friday. She said yes, quietly.

qa.q: What did Uma say when Farhan disagreed?
qa.a: 'People like him defend those parasites.'

qa.q: What might Uma's filling eyes suggest when asked about grades?
qa.a: They suggest Uma is hurting and stressed underneath the contempt, perhaps feeling like a failure.

qa.q: What did the mentor do next, and why might it help?
qa.a: Named the dehumanising words as a warning sign without arguing about videos, said they were worried, and asked Uma to meet the college counsellor together.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel after being unfollowed and lumped in with 'parasites'?
qa.a: Farhan would likely feel hurt and pushed out, losing a friend just for disagreeing.

grounding: Shows a young adult calling a whole community rats, dropping friends who disagree and watching one channel, as noticed by a mentor who names the warning.

passage:
Thursday
Watched Truth Talks till 2 am again. Everything he says makes sense. It's always them: taking our seats, our jobs, our streets.
Removed Reena from the girls' group today. She keeps posting "other side" articles. I don't need that negativity.
At dinner I said something about "those cockroaches", and my little cousin Pinky, who is seven, laughed and repeated it. "Cockroaches! Cockroaches!" Mausi went very quiet and looked at me.
I felt strange. Pinky's best friend at school is from that family down the lane. Pinky thinks cockroaches are things you squash.
I told myself it's only a word. But I haven't been able to sleep, and I didn't open Truth Talks tonight. I keep thinking of Reena's last message: "I miss you when you talk like you."
Urmila

qa.q: What did Pinky do when Urmila said 'those cockroaches'?
qa.a: Pinky laughed and repeated it: 'Cockroaches! Cockroaches!'

qa.q: What did Urmila feel when Pinky repeated the word?
qa.a: Urmila felt strange and uneasy, realising a seven-year-old now heard people as things to squash.

qa.q: What small step could Urmila take next?
qa.a: Reply to Reena, keep the channel closed, and talk to Mausi or a counsellor about the anger behind the late-night videos.

qa.q: What was it like for Mausi to hear the word at dinner?
qa.a: Mausi went very quiet and looked at Urmila, likely alarmed that such language had reached a seven-year-old at the table.

grounding: Shows a young adult hardening into us-versus-them thinking, dropping a friend and bingeing one channel, and catching the dehumanising word when a child repeats it.

passage: Every night in her room above the family shop in their small hill town, Dolma watched the same channel. A man with a calm voice explained why there were no jobs: the people from the valley town. They took the contracts, they swarmed the market, they were "rats in our grain store". After six months, Dolma watched nothing else. When Nandini, her friend since nursery, said at the bus stand, "Not all of them, Dolma, my Mama married one," Dolma turned away and stopped answering her calls. Then, at the tea shop on Sunday, Dolma heard her own voice say, "Those rats should go back." Across the room sat Mrs Rai, who had taught her maths for free for two years and came from the valley town. Mrs Rai looked down at her cup. Dolma's face burned. Rats. She had said it about a woman who once walked her home in the rain. That night she didn't open the channel. She wrote to Nandini: "Can we talk?"

qa.q: What did Nandini say at the bus stand?
qa.a: “Not all of them, Dolma, my Mama married one.”

qa.q: How did Dolma feel when Mrs Rai looked down at her cup?
qa.a: Dolma felt ashamed, her face burning, on seeing she had called a kind teacher a rat.

qa.q: What warning signs could Dolma have noticed earlier?
qa.a: The dehumanising words like rats and swarmed, watching only one channel, and cutting off Nandini for disagreeing.

qa.q: What might Mrs Rai have felt hearing the words?
qa.a: Mrs Rai likely felt hurt and small, hearing a former student she had helped speak of her people as rats.

grounding: Shows a young adult who comes to see a whole group as less than human, drops a friend who disagrees and watches one channel, until the dehumanising words land on a real person.
